subject: pathology
title: Hereditary haemolytic anaemias: membrane and enzyme defects

steps.tx: **Haemolysis** shortens red cell survival and causes anaemia with reticulocytosis, raised unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, and low haptoglobin. Chronic haemolysis produces pigment gallstones and splenomegaly from sustained red cell destruction over many years. Hereditary causes split into membrane defects, enzyme defects and haemoglobin disorders that need different counselling. Film morphology gives the fastest guide because **spherocytes**, elliptocytes, bite cells and sickle forms each name their underlying disease.
steps.say: Haemolysis raises reticulocytes, bilirubin and one enzyme marker while haptoglobin falls during active destruction. Chronic destruction stones the gallbladder and enlarges the spleen over many years of sustained haemolysis. Film shape names the cause quickly because each morphology points toward a different inherited defect.

steps.tx: **Hereditary spherocytosis** follows defects in spectrin, ankyrin or band 3 that reduce membrane surface and make red cells spherical and rigid. Spherical cells lack central pallor, show raised mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration and become trapped inside the spleen. Increased **osmotic fragility** supports the diagnosis, and splenectomy stops haemolysis although spherocytes persist on the film afterwards. Parvovirus infection can halt production and pigment gallstones complicate childhood in many affected families.
steps.say: Spherocytes lose membrane surface, become round and rigid, and die inside the spleen during passage. Fragility testing supports the diagnosis, and removing the spleen stops haemolysis although the abnormal shape persists. Affected families often develop gallstones and jaundice because chronic destruction begins early in childhood for many patients.

steps.tx: **G6PD deficiency** is an X linked enzyme defect that leaves red cells defenceless against oxidant stress from infections, fava beans, naphthalene and selected drugs. Primaquine and dapsone are classic drug triggers that cause episodic intravascular haemolysis with **Heinz bodies** and bite cells on the film. Counts normalise between crises, so the history and film during an episode carry great diagnostic weight. Enzyme assay during a crisis can falsely normalise because young reticulocytes contain more enzyme, a classic testing trap.
steps.say: This X linked defect leaves red cells defenceless whenever oxidant stress follows infection, beans or selected drugs. Heinz bodies form inside cells and the spleen bites them out during a painful haemolytic episode. Enzyme testing during a crisis misleads because young cells contain more enzyme than older cells do.

steps.tx: The film shows red cells with a semicircular defect called **bite cells** after the spleen has removed damaged haemoglobin inclusions. The inset shows dark **Heinz bodies** inside red cells, which are precipitates of oxidised haemoglobin during oxidant stress. This pairing is classic for **G6PD deficiency** during an acute haemolytic episode triggered by infection, beans or drugs. In the exam, bite cells with Heinz bodies should immediately raise oxidant haemolysis rather than membrane disease.
steps.say: This film shows bite cells where the spleen has removed damaged inclusions from circulating red cells. The inset shows dark Heinz bodies that represent oxidised haemoglobin precipitated during severe oxidant stress inside cells. Together they point toward G6PD deficiency during a crisis triggered by infection, beans or selected drugs.

steps.tx: **Pyruvate kinase deficiency** starves red cells of ATP and causes chronic haemolysis with spiky echinocytes, splenomegaly and iron overload without regular transfusion. Iron overload develops because ineffective erythropoiesis signals increase gut iron absorption over many years of disease. **Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria** is acquired rather than hereditary because a PIGA mutation removes CD55 and CD59 anchors from cell surfaces. Loss of those anchors allows complement mediated intravascular haemolysis with dark morning urine, thrombosis and marrow failure.
steps.say: Pyruvate kinase deficiency starves red cells of energy and causes lifelong haemolysis with splenic enlargement. Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is acquired because a mutation removes protective anchors and allows complement mediated destruction. Dark morning urine and unusual clots separate the acquired clone from purely inherited enzyme defects.

steps.tx: Autoimmune haemolysis must be separated from hereditary disease by the **direct antiglobulin test** that detects antibody or complement coating red cells. Warm IgG disease follows lymphoma, lupus or drugs, coats cells for splenic removal and responds to steroid treatment. Cold IgM agglutinin disease follows mycoplasma or lymphoma, fixes complement and causes acral ischaemia in cold fingers and toes. Hereditary films remain **Coombs negative**, which gives the decisive branch point in haemolysis stems.
steps.say: The Coombs test separates immune destruction from inherited disease because positive coating proves antibody mediated haemolysis. Warm disease responds to steroids and removes cells through the spleen in most patients with symptoms. Cold disease clumps cells in cold fingers, while inherited films remain negative and need morphology based sorting.
